Intel Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:INTC) AI-driven server demand offers a growth opportunity, but a deeper PC slowdown and costly foundry investments threaten its turnaround, says analyst.

Rising memory prices have been weighing on PC demand, particularly laptops, but the slowdown “came a little sooner and deeper than we thought,” Intel’s corporate vice president of investor relations, John Pitzer, told MarketWatch.

Despite progress in chip manufacturing, Intel’s latest results highlighted the challenges of turning its turnaround efforts into a “sustained recovery,” eMarketer senior analyst Asa Hiken told the publication.

Intel has benefited from a surge in data-center server CPU demand driven by the rise of agentic AI, strengthening its position in the AI market beyond traditional GPU competition. However, Hiken cautioned that the demand may not be enough to offset near-term challenges, particularly continued weakness in the PC market.

The chipmaker’s long-term growth hinges largely on its foundry business, with its advanced chip-packaging technology emerging as a promising area attracting customer interest and Wall Street optimism, Hiken said.

Hiken noted that Intel faces massive chipmaking costs and must secure significant foundry customer commitments to justify its investments and reassure investors about the business’s viability.

Weak Q4 Outlook Overshadows Earnings Beat

In the third quarter, Intel beat quarterly earnings and revenue estimates, reporting adjusted EPS of 52 cents against expectations of 40 cents and revenue of $16.51 billion versus the $16.47 billion consensus. However, its fourth-quarter guidance disappointed, with projected adjusted EPS of 25 cents and revenue of $15 billion-$16 billion, both below analyst expectations.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan said CPU demand remains “robust” despite near-term PC industry weakness, with the company prioritizing increased supply of its Xeon processors while strengthening its product lineup and roadmap to drive long-term growth and shareholder value.

Intel’s stock slumped about 23% after hours on Thursday, prompting CNBC’s Jim Cramer, who had previously called it his favorite stock, to express anger and disappointment. Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster attributed the weak outlook to slowing PC demand amid high memory costs, cautioning that Intel’s challenges should not be viewed as a warning for Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), which continues to beat estimates.

Intel Beats on Earnings and Revenue but Guides Q4 Well Below Estimates

Intel reported third-quarter earnings of 52 cents per share, beating the consensus estimate of 40 cents. It reported revenue of $16.51 billion, beating the consensus estimate of $16.47 billion. The fourth-quarter outlook is what moved the stock. Intel expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents, against the consensus estimate of 43 cents, and revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, against the consensus estimate of $17.05 billion.

"Despite near-term headwinds across the PC industry, demand for our CPUs remains robust," said Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s CEO. "Our immediate priority is to unlock additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for our Xeon family."

Why Intel’s Report Is a Read-Through for Nvidia

Nvidia’s AI accelerators are a different business from Intel’s PC and server processors, so the read-through is partly about sentiment and partly about exposure. A drop of this size in a large chipmaker pulls the group lower as investors cut positions in stocks that have run up, and Intel’s warning about PC industry headwinds adds to the questions.

Nvidia also owns about 214.8 million Intel shares, bought for $5 billion at $23.28 each in a deal completed in December, and the two companies are developing x86 RTX chips for PCs and custom x86 CPUs for data centers. The stake was valued at about $30.0 billion on June 30, according to Nvidia’s filing, and at Intel’s extended-trading price of $76.85 it would be worth about $16.5 billion. On the other side, Tan said demand for Intel’s server CPUs is extraordinary, which fits with strong AI infrastructure spending.

Nvidia Reports in Mid-November, With Analysts Expecting About $108.8B in Revenue

Nvidia is expected to report fiscal third-quarter results after the market closes on Nov. 17. Analysts estimate earnings per share of $2.48 along with revenue of $109.17 billion. Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) stock fell more than 7% in Friday’s premarket trading as investors weighed accelerating cloud growth against soaring AI spending and mounting retail risks.

The selloff came amid broader weakness in technology stocks, with Nasdaq futures falling 2.35% and S&P 500 futures declining 0.99%.

Amazon shares had already lost more than 4% Thursday as analysts raised concerns about capital spending, cash flow and the growing threat of AI-powered shopping assistants.

Amazon Misses Estimates Despite AWS Surge

Amazon reported third-quarter revenue of $201.94 billion, missing Wall Street’s estimate of $202.31 billion. Earnings of $1.89 per share fell short of expectations of $1.97.

Revenue rose 12% year over year, while Amazon Web Services (AWS) sales surged 39% to $46 billion, marking the cloud division’s fastest growth in nearly five years.

Amazon forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, compared with the $244.51 billion consensus estimate.

CEO Andy Jassy expects AWS revenue growth to exceed 40% in both 2027 and 2028.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Wall Street Sees $220 Billion Spending Challenge

Blue Line Capital’s Bill Baruch told CNBC that Amazon’s biggest challenge was determining when its massive capital spending would peak.

He cited approximately $220 billion in capital expenditures this year, warning that investors needed greater visibility into future spending.

Still, Baruch said AWS growth reaching the low-40% range could support shares. He highlighted Amazon’s roughly $496 billion backlog, Trainium chips and Bedrock platform as potential catalysts.

Evercore ISI’s Mark Mahaney also identified AWS growth as the critical metric, alongside cloud margins and backlog expansion.

Mahaney warned that aggressive AI investment had weakened free cash flow expectations across major cloud providers.

However, he said Amazon appeared capable of financing its expansion, citing approximately $100 billion in debt raised over the previous 12 months.

Retail Weakness And AI Shopping Threaten Growth

Maxim Group’s Tom Forte, who maintained a Buy rating and $350 price forecast, warned that higher gasoline prices and pressure on consumers could weigh on Amazon’s holiday shopping performance.

Forte also flagged potential competition from a DoorDash-Instacart combination and the growing adoption of AI-powered shopping assistants.

Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster told CNBC Amazon’s stock decline reflected legitimate retail concerns, including the risk that personalized AI shopping bots could disrupt its business beginning in late 2027.

However, Munster viewed Amazon’s multiyear AWS growth outlook as an unusually strong signal of sustained AI demand.

He also said growing demand for Amazon’s Trainium chips could challenge Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), even as broader cloud expansion benefits AI infrastructure providers.

The Trump administration is reportedly preparing a new national security measure aimed at limiting Chinese telecom companies’ access to American phone numbers and disrupting scam-related robocalls.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is scheduled to vote Nov. 19 on a proposal that could block China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other internet-based providers from directly accessing U.S. phone numbers, Reuters reported on Thursday.

For telecom companies providing Voice over Internet Protocol, direct access is ⁠a cheaper option and makes it easier to offer advanced features, the report added. The agency said restricting that access would reinforce protections against illegal robocalls.

The agency may revoke existing direct-number authorizations for Chinese companies considered security risks, according to the report. The FCC has already prohibited the three named telecom providers from offering international telecommunications services to the U.S.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr told the publication that the decision would strengthen the agency’s "first line of defense" against "bad actors and illegal robocallers."

The FCC also intends to limit providers that use equipment from companies on its national security risk list, including Huawei and ZTE. Chinese laboratories could additionally be barred from testing U.S. electronics beginning in December 2028.

China’s foreign ministry said Friday that it firmly opposed the expected ban, accusing Washington of broadening national security justifications and using government authority to suppress Chinese companies.

FCC did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Was Target of Chinese Intelligence Asset, Raising Questions Over Potential AI Chip Diversion: Report

US Expands Scrutiny Of Chinese Tech

The proposal extends a broader U.S. effort to scrutinize Chinese-linked communications infrastructure.

Earlier this month, Washington was also considering restrictions on Chinese optical transceivers, components that move data through fiber-optic networks and support artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Shares of Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE) and Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR) rose after reports of those potential measures.

In June, the FCC proposed tighter oversight of submarine cables, which carry about 99% of international internet traffic, creating more room for U.S. tech giants, including Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), to expand networks.

Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) is expanding its Bedrock AI platform with China’s Kimi and GLM open models, while CEO Andy Jassy outlined ambitions for the service to eventually match Amazon’s massive EC2 cloud business.

Amazon disclosed the additions during its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, adding to Bedrock’s mix of proprietary and open AI models. Jassy said Bedrock now offers closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI, alongside open models such as Moonshot‘s Kimi K3 and Z.ai‘s GLM 5.3. He also referenced Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX)  SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 model on Bedrock.

"The Western world is very hungry for additional open models that are Western open models," Jassy said, adding, “I believe that will happen over time as well.”

He called Bedrock’s potential "gigantic," suggesting the platform could ultimately become comparable in scale to Amazon Web Services’ EC2, a core cloud computing offering. Jassy also emphasized Bedrock’s security structure, saying customer inputs and outputs are not shared with model providers or used to train their foundational models. He expects six to eight models to handle more than 95% of workloads within two to three years.

China’s AI Models Challenge US Rivals

Amazon’s model expansion follows the broader rise of Chinese-developed open AI systems. Earlier this month, Amazon Bedrock added Z.ai’s GLM 5.3 open-weight model, offering customers enhanced capabilities for agentic coding and complex software engineering with AWS security and compliance protections.

Last week, former Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China was roughly six months behind the U.S. in AI, but warned that free products could still give China a strategic advantage. He said China’s cheaper, often free and open-weight AI models could gain traction in developing markets, while attributing the country’s progress partly to access to restricted advanced chips and the use of distillation to replicate capabilities of Western AI systems.

In July, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), called Chinese models "excellent" and argued that Washington should use rather than ban high-quality open-source technology. Huang dismissed fears that Chinese open AI models pose security risks or threaten U.S. tech firms. He argued that wider adoption of models like DeepSeek and Kimi will boost demand for Nvidia chips and infrastructure, saying Wall Street has repeatedly underestimated their impact.

Alphabet, Inc’s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) shares plunged nearly 13% on Thursday, wiping out about $482 billion in market value. It was the second-largest one-day loss ever recorded for a U.S.-listed company, behind Nvidia’s $593 billion wipeout in January 2025.

The selloff followed Alphabet’s third-quarter results, which raised concerns about whether its massive artificial intelligence investments are generating sufficient returns.

The concerns extend beyond Alphabet. Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) reported 39% growth in AWS revenue, but its trailing 12-month free cash flow fell to a record outflow of more than $42 billion, reflecting increased infrastructure spending.

For ETF investors, the question is whether growing exposure to mega-cap technology companies could amplify losses as investors reassess the returns on AI investments.

Read Also: Alphabet Bulls Dig in After Messy Q3: 'AI Stack Keeps Us Bullish' Cantor Says

QQQ and XLC face concentration risks

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is particularly exposed to this trend. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet and Amazon are among its largest holdings, making it vulnerable to a broader reassessment of AI valuations and spending.

The Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLC) faces even greater direct Alphabet exposure. Its two share classes together account for a substantial portion of the portfolio, alongside Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META).

Thursday’s trading highlighted the impact of these exposures. XLC fell 1.87%, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLK) declined 1.18%. The broader SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) lost 0.37%.

Could Equal-Weight ETFs Offer a Buffer?

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) gained 1.2% on Thursday, even as SPY declined 0.37%.

Unlike traditional market-cap-weighted funds, RSP assigns approximately equal weights to S&P 500 constituents, limiting the influence of individual mega-cap stocks on portfolio performance.

Another alternative is the Invesco NASDAQ 100 Equal Weighted ETF (NASDAQ:QQQE), which provides exposure to Nasdaq-100 companies without allowing the largest constituents to dominate.

However, equal weighting is not necessarily safer. It can increase exposure to smaller, more volatile companies and underperform when mega-cap stocks lead the market.

Market Volatility Becomes Difficult to Ignore

U.S.-listed stocks suffered 18 sessions in 2026 when at least $200 billion in market value was erased—more than the 13 recorded in all of 2025 and more than any year before 2022.

As AI infrastructure spending rises, investors may increasingly distinguish between companies translating AI investments into revenue and those struggling to generate sufficient cash flow.

For ETF investors, portfolio concentration could matter as much as choosing which sector to own.

Despite Donald Trump‘s recent claims that inflation has sharply declined, the Federal Reserve continues to warn that consumer prices are still running uncomfortably high.

Trump’s Economic Claims

On Oct. 30, Trump posted on social media that inflation is “way down” under his leadership. In the same publication, Trump stated that income for people and companies is “way up” and declared that “The Golden Age of America Is Upon Us”.

Read Also: Kevin Warsh Views Economy as 'Strong' and 'Pointing in the Right Direction': Crypto Bettors Weigh Recession Odds

Federal Reserve’s Assessment

Trump’s statements contrast with the assessments provided by the Federal Reserve earlier in the week. On Oct. 28, the Federal Open Market Committee released a statement noting that “Inflation remains elevated.”

During a press conference the same day, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh stated that “Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the Committee’s objective for close to 6 years.”

Warsh added that “inflation is too high” and noted that “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks”. Warsh also stated that “It’s our responsibility to get inflation down”.

The Sept. 15-16, 2026, Federal Open Market Committee minutes indicated that recent price increases were driven by “the effects of past tariff increases, higher energy and input costs stemming from geopolitical developments, and an increase in technology-related consumer goods prices associated with the AI buildout.”

Monetary Policy Stance

To address economic conditions, the Federal Open Market Committee announced on October 28, 2026, that it “decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4%.”

The committee stated that the “accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal.” The Federal Reserve reaffirmed that “The Committee will deliver price stability.”

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 12.57% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 12.69%, and the Dow Jones gained 8.19% YTD.

Hilton criticized Zuckerberg for allegedly seeking “Meta carve-outs” from a potential one-party government.

“The sad thing is that your business may be one of the few that can continue to operate here, and you may be one of the few that can afford to live here!,” he wrote, addressing the Meta CEO.

Hilton warned that continued Democratic rule could hurt businesses and make California unaffordable for most people. “The business exodus of recent years could turn into a stampede,” he wrote.

Meta did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Meta-Backed PAC Donates $1 Million to Becerra

The allegation followed a New York Post report that a Meta-backed super political action committee (PAC) had made a last-minute $1 million contribution to Becerra’s California gubernatorial campaign. The report described the money as coming from a super PAC backed by Zuckerberg, placing the contribution in the final stretch of the campaign. 

Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (META) California donated nearly $1 million to Xavier Becerra’s campaign in five installments between Oct. 20 and 27, bringing its total contributions to more than $2.2 million, the report stated, citing campaign finance records.

Xavier Becerra, former HHS Secretary under the Biden administration, is running against Republican Steve Hilton in the race to succeed California Governor Gavin Newsom.

California’s Regulatory Impact on Big Tech

California’s gubernatorial race matters to the tech industry because the state can shape regulations on AI, social media, and other sectors where major companies like Meta operate.

Last week, Meta agreed to grant Zuckerberg non-voting shares that he could sell to cover a potential multibillion-dollar California billionaire wealth tax, in exchange for an eight-year commitment to remain in the state or wherever Meta is headquartered. The arrangement would allow Zuckerberg to retain voting control while potentially selling shares to meet the tax bill if voters approve Proposition 40. Meta’s board committee said keeping Zuckerberg in leadership is critical amid intensifying AI competition.

Bank of America’s top strategist has found value in an unloved corner of the AI trade: the bonds of the companies paying for it.

“Buy tech bond ‘diamonds-in-rough’ as AI hyperscalers up equity issuance, cut buybacks,” Michael Hartnett, chief investment strategist at Bank of America, said in his latest Flow Show note.

The call comes after a punishing year for tech credit.

Why Hartnett Calls Tech Bonds ‘Diamonds in the Rough’

According to Hartnett, U.S. technology bonds have lost about 9% so far in 2026.

That leaves their total return relative to the broad investment-grade bond index at the lowest level in 30 years. In other words, tech debt has rarely looked this cheap compared with the rest of the high-grade market.

The main reason is supply. AI hyperscalers have sold $182 billion of bonds this year, up from just $17 billion in 2024, as they borrow to build data centers.

Investors have demanded higher yields to absorb that wave. As a result, long-dated bonds of the Magnificent Seven and other AI leaders now yield between 6% and 8%, a level Hartnett considers attractive.

Further down the credit ladder, the 2031 high-yield bond of CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) yields 14.26%.

Read Also: Nvidia's Credit Risk Has Tripled This Year — and Just Passed Meta's

Why Bondholders Are Gaining the Upper Hand

The second part of Hartnett’s argument concerns how the hyperscalers are now raising money.

Meta’s recent share sale, he said, signals a new respect for credit investors. Selling stock rather than adding more debt strengthens the balance sheet that bondholders rely on.

Hartnett also believes the long stretch in which AI bonds lagged AI stocks is coming to an end.

Hyperscalers have raised $89 billion through equity issuance in 2026. At the same time, their share buybacks are running at an annualized pace of just $14 billion, down from $105 billion in 2024.

For Hartnett, that means the era of big stock buybacks is over. Cash that used to flow back to shareholders is now being kept inside the companies, which in turn favors those who own the debt.

The pressure comes from spending. Bank of America estimates AI capital expenditure will climb from $240 billion in 2024 to $1.2 trillion in 2027. Over the same period, free cash flow is seen swinging from $240 billion to negative $180 billion.

For this reason, Hartnett said, bond markets are now policing the AI boom.

S&P Global Data Show Credit Markets Are Still Nervous

The bond market has not given the all-clear yet.

Five-year credit default swaps, which show the annual cost of insuring a company’s debt against default, have widened sharply across Big Tech since early September, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data as of Friday.

Oracle’s spread rose to 276 basis points from 210 on Sept. 1. Nvidia’s climbed to 129 from 84, while Meta’s increased to 118 from 94.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) moved to 85 from 61, and Amazon to 90 from 67. Microsoft remained the safest name, at 55 from 47.

However, there are early signs of stabilization. Oracle’s spread has eased from a peak of 325 basis points on Oct. 20.

S&P Global has flagged a deeper shift. In an Oct. 13 update, it said spreads on AI-exposed tech companies have widened even as the broader investment-grade market has held up.

Investors, S&P Global said, increasingly treat AI exposure as a distinct credit risk. In addition, rising correlations among hyperscalers, chipmakers and other AI issuers mean tech credit is starting to trade as a single theme, eroding the diversification benefits of holding several names.

Supply will not fade soon. S&P Global said hyperscaler-related bond issuance reached about $240 billion in the first three quarters, on pace for its $250 billion to $300 billion full-year estimate.

Read Also: Fed's Warsh Falls Short of Calling a December Hike: The Market Is Doing It for Him

The Levels Hartnett Is Watching

Hartnett expects risk-off conditions to persist until the global rate-hiking cycle ends. Central banks have delivered 42 hikes over the past six months.

He sees a release valve in the first half of 2027: geopolitical peace, a collapse in oil prices and the end of rate hikes.

Before any year-end rally, Hartnett said two levels must hold: $70 on the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (CBOE:MAGS) and $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH).

On Friday, MAGS slipped 2.2% to $69.70, just below that line. SMH remains about 8% above its threshold.

Treasury yields offer little relief. The 10-year yield stood at 4.93% and the 30-year at 5.29%. The iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (NYSE:LQD) is down 5.5% this year.

Hartnett’s case rests on a simple shift. Shareholders have funded the AI race so far. Now bondholders are being paid more to finance the next leg, even as default-protection costs show that credit markets remain wary.

Wall Street banks favor enormous AI financing deals while smaller GPU operators struggle to borrow, USD.AI co-founder Conor Moore told Benzinga in an exclusive interview.

“The banks have gotten drunk on these large IG deals because you don’t have to have a directional view or thesis on the space to be comfortable doing them,” Moore said, referring to investment-grade financing.

When Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) backs a project, lenders can focus on its ability to pay rather than whether the underlying AI business will succeed.

But the sheer volume of borrowing is testing investors’ appetite. Large bond buyers face limits on their exposure to individual companies, while the flood of AI debt is pushing them to demand higher yields.

Moore illustrated that fatigue by imagining investors saying: “I don’t have appetite for the 12th Microsoft $40 billion financing, I am tapped out of appetite.”

Wall Street’s AI Deals Stretch Lenders

Monday’s $63 billion Anthropic financing illustrates the scale of these transactions. Bank of America Corp. (NYSE:BAC), Citigroup Inc. (NYSE:C) and Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) are arranging senior loans for Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) AI chips, with Blackstone Inc. (NYSE:BX) providing junior financing.

Several banks considered withdrawing before Broadcom offered better terms, including protection against falling equipment values.

Bank of America also struggled to syndicate a $14 billion loan for an Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) data center in Michigan and turned to long-term bond investors instead, Karen Fang, the bank’s global head of infrastructure and sustainable finance, told BloombergNEF. She said capital remains available for strong projects.

Moore said that pressure is forcing lenders to be "more creative and thoughtful about what deals they’re doing and actually have a directional view on the underlying business."

Who Finances Smaller AI Companies?

USD.AI arranges GPU-backed loans of $20 million to $250 million. Moore expects average deals to rise from roughly $50 million to $100 million.

Smaller operators can deploy GPUs in converted telecom buildings or shipping containers, tapping existing power supplies and potentially avoiding lengthy construction delays.

But their loans are harder for traditional lenders to assess. “The market is starving for standardization,” Moore said.

USD.AI aims to make these loans easier to evaluate, attracting private-credit funds, family offices and eventually regional banks and insurers.

On Polymarket, traders put the odds of an AI industry downturn at roughly 10% by December 31 and 23% by June 30, 2027. The market requires three major distress events within 90 days.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) also has an interest in expanding access to GPU financing.

In August, Nvidia announced partnerships aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion in third-party AI infrastructure funding.

But lenders remain concerned about GPU depreciation, while financing constraints could slow chip purchases by smaller operators.

Moore said USD.AI scores each deal out of 100 on the operator, its customers and the contract itself, rejecting anything below 60.

Loan funds also sit in escrow and aren’t released until servers are installed in the data center, a rule Moore said ensures "the transaction is derisked."

The federal government’s stake in Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) lost roughly $12 billion in paper value Friday as the chipmaker’s shares collapsed.

  • INTC stock is tanking. Get all the details here. 

Intel shares sank about 30% to roughly $64 on Friday morning after issuing weaker-than-expected guidance and pointing to ongoing softness in the PC market. The stock was headed for its worst single session ever, and the selloff landed hard on Washington, which owns nearly a tenth of the company. 

In August 2025, the Commerce Department acquired 433.3 million Intel shares at $20.47 each. The deal gave the government a 9.9% stake for roughly $9 billion. 

Intel closed Thursday at $92.07, valuing the position at about $39.9 billion, per Benzinga Pro data. At $64 a share, the holding fell to roughly $27.7 billion. 

The one-day hit comes to about $12.2 billion.

The damage looks worse against Intel’s peak. A months-long rally pushed the stake’s value as high as $61 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported. From that level, the government has now given back more than $33 billion. 

Read Also: Bears Load Up on Ondas, Dutch Bros and 8 More Stocks — Is a Squeeze Brewing?

Guidance Drives the INTC Drop

Intel said it expects fourth quarter adjusted EPS of 25 cents, versus the 43 cent analyst estimate, and revenue in a range of $15 billion to $16 billion, versus the $17.05 billion consensus. CFO David Zinsner said he expects the PC slowdown to last at least through the first half of next year. 

Before the earnings report, Intel stock had climbed about 150% in 2026. October had already erased roughly 23% as investors grew uneasy about the size of the artificial intelligence buildout. 

The broader market offered no cushion as the Nasdaq futures dropped over 2% as Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) also slid after earnings, capping a rough week for tech results. 

Other Backers Feel it Too

Washington is not alone. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and SoftBank Group also invested billions in Intel last year.

Still Deep in the Green

Even after the rout, U.S. taxpayers hold a paper gain of about $18.9 billion on Intel. The stake remains worth more than three times its cost.

Intel anchors a much broader federal portfolio. The government has announced 43 deals involving stock or warrants convertible into equity, totaling around $30 billion, according to Council on Foreign Relations data cited by the Wall Street Journal. 

Intel is by far the largest, leaving the portfolio’s headline returns tethered to a single volatile stock.

Wall Street remains overwhelmingly bullish on artificial intelligence despite mounting evidence of financing problems, Barclays PLC (NYSE:BCS) strategist Alexander “Alty” Altmann warned.

“We’re in the denial phase right now because everyone is still extremely bullish,” Altmann, Barclays’ global head of equities tactical strategies, said on Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast episode released Thursday.

Altmann noted that subprime financing trouble appeared 12 to 24 months before the 2008 financial crisis reached major banks.

He sees a potential parallel in AI, where data-center builders with little operating cash flow borrow billions while cash-rich customers such as Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) keep spending.

He stressed he wasn’t making a direct comparison.

The First Cracks Are Already Appearing

Altmann pointed to Cipher Digital Inc. (NASDAQ:CIFR), which proposed $850 million in convertible notes on Oct. 13 alongside a debt-for-shares exchange. Its shares fell nearly 13% amid dilution concerns.

He said the anxiety spread to CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV), an AI cloud provider that borrows heavily to build data centers.

CoreWeave co-founder Brannin McBee had also discussed tapping insurers for cheaper financing as the company sought to fund its rapid expansion.

CoreWeave’s bond yields climbed toward 15% in mid-October, up from 9.675% when issued. Higher borrowing costs could squeeze returns even if demand stays strong.

Altmann said spreads on data-center bonds, including financing tied to Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), had already been widening for months.

“There is evidently a financing problem within neoclouds,” he said, referring to specialized AI cloud providers.

Yet only about 60% of respondents to a preliminary Barclays investor survey expected financing problems. Altmann argued the figure should have been 100%, showing how Wall St is still in denial that AI financing is in trouble.

AI Borrowers Face a Crowded Market

Altmann warned that AI companies are competing for financing in an already crowded debt market.

Barclays expects $1.1 trillion in net corporate bond issuance this year, even as interest rates remain elevated.

“AI is not issuing debt in a vacuum,” Altmann said.

Altmann agreed that lenders are becoming more selective, making it harder and more expensive for heavily indebted AI companies to fund their expansion.

Altmann said a major hyperscaler cutting planned capital spending could finally shake investors’ confidence, although he suggested that might not happen until next year.

On Polymarket, traders put the odds of an AI industry downturn at 9% by Dec. 31, rising to 23% by June 30. The contract requires three major distress events within 90 days, a far more severe outcome than the financing problems Altmann describes.

For CoreWeave and its peers, financing pressure has arrived before their biggest customers have even begun cutting spending.

Semiconductor stocks lost roughly $1 trillion in market value on Friday, and just five companies did most of the damage.

By 11:35 a.m. ET, 23 of the world’s largest chipmakers and equipment suppliers had shed about $1.01 trillion across Wall Street and Asia. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC), Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE:TSM) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) alone accounted for $610 billion of that, or about 60%.

The trigger was Intel. Its shares plunged 28.4% to $65.92 after the chipmaker’s fourth-quarter outlook landed well short of expectations. If the drop holds, it would be the stock’s steepest one-day fall since July 1974.

Five Chip Stocks Drove 60% of the Selloff

Nvidia led in dollar terms. Its shares fell only 3.6%, yet that move erased about $185 billion, because Nvidia is worth close to $5 trillion.

Intel fell nearly eight times as hard in percentage terms. However, it lost less money, about $138 billion.

TSMC dropped 5.4%, wiping out roughly $108 billion. Broadcom slid 5.5% and AMD sank 9.7%, and each shed about $90 billion.

Elsewhere, SK Hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY) closed 7.1% lower in Seoul, erasing about $64 billion. Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), down 5.2%, lost $55 billion.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) tumbled 8%, on track for its worst day since early June. The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 7.1%, its second drop of more than 6% in just over a week.

Intel’s AI Boom Has a Supply Problem

Intel’s Data Center and AI division grew revenue 78% to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in 15 years. However, shortages of wafers and substrates are capping server shipments, and relief is not expected until the second half of 2027.

Meanwhile, the PC business is shrinking. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the roughly $17.1 billion analysts expected. It also warned the slowdown would last through the first half of 2027.

The culprit is high memory-chip prices. These are the same prices that lifted SK Hynix, Micron and Sandisk Corp. (NASDAQ:SNDK) this year. Now they are making PCs too expensive to sell in volume.

“Intel’s forward outlook proved to be a perfect storm,” Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse said in a note. He called the implied 45% year-over-year collapse in PC units a meaningful surprise. He also cut his price target to $90 from $125 and kept a Neutral rating.

Bank of America Securities analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut his price objective to $100 from $145. Arya said strong demand for server processors tied to agentic AI is more than offset by PC and supply headwinds.

Why the Whole Sector Paid

On Thursday, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) suffered its worst day on record. On Friday, Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) fell 1.3% after its third-quarter revenue came in slightly below estimates.

As a result, investors are again questioning when the hundreds of billions spent on AI infrastructure will pay off.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said on X that AI’s disruption is now visible in tech earnings. He still sees 2027 as the year AI revenue starts to justify the spending.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.9%, and the S&P 500 lost 1.4%. The 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.95%, while the 30-year yield rose 2 basis points to 5.32%.

Five stocks generated 60% of Friday’s chip losses. The same concentration that lifted semiconductor indexes on the way up is now working in reverse.

Nvidia alone shed about $212 billion as it fell 4.1%, while AMD dropped 11.1% and Qualcomm 11.0%.

Oil extended its rally after reports of a tanker attack near the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.1% to $104.14 a barrel, and Brent gained 2.4% to $113.44.

Precious metals went the other way. Gold fell 3.1% to $3,908.10 an ounce, its lowest level since early October 2025, as traders weighed the risk of another Federal Reserve hike after two officials dissented in favor of an increase this week. Silver lost 5.9% to $49.28, back below $50.
